Als ich im August 2019 zum ersten Mal die Werkstatt in der Hohenzollernstraße betrat, wusste ich noch nicht, dass dieser Ort mein Leben verändern würde. Mein Onkel Klaus hatte dort ein kleines Reparaturgeschäft für Fahrräder und Motorroller, und ich verbrachte jeden Nachmittag zwischen Ölkannen und Werkzeugkisten. Eines Tages brachte eine Kundin einen alten Passat mit dem Kennzeichen ZZ-CD 2307, der seit Wochen nicht mehr anspringen wollte. Ich durfte die Elektronik prüfen, und nach drei Stunden Fehlersuche fanden wir ein durchgescheuertes Kabel am Zündschloss. Dieses Erfolgserlebnis hat mich mehr geprägt als jede Note in der Schule.

Seitdem dokumentiere ich meine Projekte auf meinem Kanal unter dem Namen @klaus_schraubt, wo ich Schritt für Schritt zeige, wie man Fehler systematisch eingrenzt. Die Resonanz hat mich überrascht: Zuschauer aus Düsseldorf, Kiel und sogar aus München schreiben mir, wenn sie selbst an einem Problem hängen. Klaus sagt immer, dass gute Mechanik mit Geduld beginnt, nicht mit Werkzeug. Dieser Satz begleitet mich bis heute.

Ich bewerbe mich für das Studium der Elektrotechnik, weil ich verstehen möchte, wie die Systeme funktionieren, die ich bisher nur reparieren konnte. Ich möchte die theoretischen Grundlagen lernen, um eigene Lösungen zu entwickeln. Am 14. August 2024 werde ich volljährig, und ich freue mich darauf, diesen neuen Abschnitt mit einer klaren Richtung zu beginnen.

Hi, I'm Alex Turner and I need some advice. I grew up in Springfield, Indiana, but for the past six years I've been living in Indianapolis, and my mom keeps guilt-tripping me about not coming home more. Last November she had a fall and I flew back, and now I can't stop thinking that I should move back to Springfield permanently. My job here is good and my friends are here, though, and I don't know how to explain to my wife, Maya, that I'm torn. Every time I bring it up she gets quiet and says she doesn't want to uproot her life for my family drama. How do I talk to her without it turning into a fight? I'd really appreciate any practical steps.

Dear Journal,

I keep telling myself that the panic attacks are getting less frequent, but last Thursday on the Rue des Étoiles I had to stand against a shop window for twenty minutes before I could breathe properly. Céline from the office found me, sat down on the kerb beside me without asking questions, and walked me back to my flat in the Saint-Germain. She said I should write things down, so here I am. Dr. Laurent wants me to track the triggers: crowds, the metro at rush hour, unanswered emails. My registration for the Renault is CD-789-PL if I need to remember where I parked, and my client portal login is claudine.bourgeois@lumiere-conseil.fr, which I check far too often.

Session went well on the 4th of December. Dr. Laurent asked me to name one thing I did for myself that week, and I said I had bought a proper notebook, which made her smile. We talked about my national ID, 12 34 56 78 901 00, which I had to dig out for the bank and which made me feel oddly exposed, as if my whole life were a file. I am trying to notice that feeling instead of obeying it.

Céline has invited me to the Canal Saint-Martin on Sunday, and I think I will go, even if I leave early. Writing this has helped more than I expected. Tomorrow I will try to write one thing I am grateful for, even a small one. The bread from the corner bakery counts.

C.

I am a systems engineer who has spent most of my career building reliable infrastructure for small teams that cannot afford downtime. My work focuses on observability, incident response and making complex distributed systems easier to reason about. Outside the office I mentor junior developers, contribute to open-source tooling and spend too many weekends experimenting with home automation. I believe the best technical talks are the ones that admit what did not work, so expect a few honest failures alongside the lessons learned. At this conference I hope to exchange ideas with people facing the same tradeoffs between speed, cost and resilience, and to hear how others keep their on-call rotations sustainable.

Dear Grandma Ruth,

I hope this letter finds you well and that the cold in Ohio isn't bothering your knees too much. I think about you every time I pass the kitchen and smell cinnamon, which is just what I'd expect from you. Mom says you've been busy with the church bake sale committee again, and I can only imagine how many pies that involved.

I wanted to tell you some news before Thanksgiving so you'd have time to brag about me to your friends at bingo. I finally got accepted into the nursing program at Willow Creek Memorial Hospital's training partnership, starting in January. Me, a nurse! I still remember you telling me I had steady hands when I helped you thread that needle for your quilt. Dad says I have to be at the orientation on November 14th, so I'm pretty nervous but mostly excited.

I also started a job at Pine Ridge Logistics last month, answering phones and helping with scheduling. My manager, Gary Lindqvist, is strict but fair, and the people there are kind. Mostly I'm writing because I'm turning 19 this year and I wanted you to know how much your advice has stuck with me. I still keep your note in my wallet. Please give Grandpa Walt a hug from me, and call when you have a minute so we can talk properly.

All my love,  
Gracie

After nine years at Westfield Logistics, I've made the decision to step into a new chapter. On Monday 18 May I start as Senior Operations Lead at Seabrook Freight in Warrington, and I wanted to share a bit about why.

When I joined Westfield at 27, I was a coordinator who loved spreadsheets and was honestly a bit scared of meetings. Nine years later I've led three regional rollouts, managed a team of fourteen, and learned more from the people on the dock than from any course. I'm grateful for every one of those years, and for the leaders who backed me when I made mistakes.

So why move? Mostly because I want to build something from the ground up again. Seabrook is growing fast across Melbourne and into Wagga, and the role gives me a chance to shape how a team scales rather than just keep the machine running. The conversations in the interview felt like a real partnership, and that matters to me more than a title.

I also know that change is hard for the people around you. If you're on my team at Westfield, thank you. I'll be keeping in touch, and I'm happy to talk through anything you're weighing up in your own career. Feel free to reach out at vanessa.drummond@westfield.com.au before I leave on 5 May.

If you've made a similar leap, I'd love to hear how it went for you. What did you wish you'd known before you started? Drop your advice in the comments. I'll be reading every one.

On to the next chapter, and thank you for being part of this one.
